content_ta: TeraWulf நிறுவனத்தின் CEO Paul Prager, சமீபத்திய தொழில்நுட்ப சந்தை சரிவு நிறுவனத்தின் பங்கின் விலையை மட்டுமே பாதித்துள்ளதாகவும், தரவு மையங்களுக்கான உண்மையான தேவையை பாதிக்கவில்லை என்றும் தெரிவித்துள்ளார். சந்தை அழுத்தம் இருந்தபோதிலும், Muskie மையத்திற்கு இன்னும் வாடகைதாரர் இல்லை என்றாலும், AI உள்கட்டமைப்புக்கான அடிப்படை தேவையில் தலைமைத்துவம் நம்பிக்கையுடன் உள்ளது.

title: Iliad Solutions Targets South African Banking and Payments Market
summary:
Iliad Solutions, a global leader in payment testing, is stepping up its efforts to develop business in South Africa, targeting banks, financial services organisations and software providers seeking to improve the reliability of their payment systems.
The expansion builds on the appointment of South African banking and payments specialist Jill Murtagh, who will help Iliad identify commercial opportunities, develop relationships with decision-makers and navigate the local market.
As payment infrastructure evolves at speed, a new regulatory regime is introduced (which allows broader participation in the payments ecosystem), and financial institutions introduce additional services, testing has become an increasingly important part of managing operational risk. Iliad provides specialist payment testing technology to help organisations validate systems, identify issues and reduce the risk of disruption when changes are introduced. It also provides standardisation of testing and assistance with pre-certification into the payment rails.
Anthony Walton, CEO, Iliad Solutions, said: “South Africa offers a compelling opportunity for Iliad. Its banking and payments sector has considerable depth, and we believe our technology can help organisations address the challenges of developing and maintaining reliable payment systems.
“Jill knows the market from the inside. Her experience in banking operations and domestic and cross-border payments gives us a strong starting point as we build relationships and identify where our testing solutions can deliver real value.”
Jill Murtagh spent 23 years at Bidvest Bank as Executive Head of Payments and Banking Operations, helping establish its banking operations and end-to-end payment infrastructure. Her experience spans domestic and cross-border payments, operational support and strategic payment gateways.
She will focus on connecting Iliad with prospective customers and technology partners, understanding their requirements and developing a qualified sales pipeline.
Iliad's initial focus will be on identifying organisations where specialist testing can support payment system development, integration and modernisation. The company aims to build its presence through local relationships and opportunities that align with its expertise.
Anthony Walton added: “Our priority is to understand what banks and payment providers need, then demonstrate how we can help. We have the specialist payment testing technology and experience; working with the right people locally will be key to turning that into business.”

title: FCA Warns AI Agent Builders They May Need Authorisation to Handle Customers’ Money
summary:
The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has warned that technology firms building AI agents that move money, arrange borrowing or make investment decisions for consumers may need its authorisation, as personal AI agents move from testing towards launch in the UK.
Setting out its expectations for firms, technology providers and social media platforms, the regulator said some agentic products will need authorisation at launch and others as their capabilities grow. It is already speaking to firms planning to offer them to UK consumers.
FCA said it supports the use of agentic AI and that it could widen access to financial tools and information. But it said products that act on a customer’s behalf can blur the line between regulated and unregulated activity, and with it the protections people get over their money and data.
For that reason, businesses must understand when AI systems go beyond providing information and start carrying out regulated activities such as moving money on behalf of customers. Depending on what an agent does, that activity could fall under payment services, financial promotions, credit broking or financial advice rules. The FCA was clear that calling a business a technology provider does not remove the need for authorisation, adding: “We have powers to intervene if we believe regulated financial services are being offered without our authorisation.”
Andrew Bud, founder & CEO, iProov, commented: “The FCA’s warning is welcome. As consumers begin using AI agents to move money, arrange loans, and make investment decisions, and financial institutions use AI to respond to such orders, regulatory clarity on accountability for both financial institutions and technology providers is very timely.”
“With banks like JPMorgan Chase already restricting certain AI agents, the need for robust safeguards is clear. Financial institutions must know who an agent represents, what it is authorised to do, and when high-risk transactions require secure human authorisation. Insisting that real people, whether consumers or staff, control specific agent actions will on occasion be essential in order to assure accountability, and banks would then have a duty to assure this.”
“Greater AI autonomy must not come at the expense of human oversight. Only real people can take accountability and provide a source of trust.”
Where a regulated firm develops or deploys agentic AI, or relies on a third-party provider, responsibility for compliance stays with the firm and its senior managers, and the Consumer Duty applies in full. The FCA said firms must understand how autonomous their systems are and how they behave under stress. They should also work out how they will verify they are dealing with an AI agent, what consents and permissions it holds, how customers get support when something goes wrong, and whether to accept payments instructed by an agent.
Matt Flenley, Head of Product and Marketing at Datactics, commented: “The real test for agentic AI in banking is what happens when the records disagree. If a customer asks an agent to move money, can the bank show which customer and account it matched, what permission it relied on and why it let the payment proceed? If two records point to different answers, the agent should pause and hand the case to someone who can resolve it. That’s where record matching, data validation and an audit trail become part of protecting the customer.”
The statement follows a joint statement on personal AI agents from the Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum (DRCF) regulators – the CMA, FCA, ICO and Ofcom – on 30 October, and a joint letter to ministers on 16 November warning that several personal AI agent products are due to launch in the UK.
The FCA said it will update its guidance as agentic products roll out. Firms can test products through its AI Lab, and the regulator plans a dedicated Agentic Policy Sprint bringing together firms, policymakers and technology providers, with expressions of interest now open.

title: Conferma Extends Virtual Card Payment Capability for Inbound International Hotel Bookings in Mainland China
summary:
Conferma, the global leader in virtual card payments, is extending its virtual card payment capability to participating hotels in mainland China through a new partnership with Fang Cang Group (FCG), a leading China-based travel technology group specialising in connectivity to local hotel supply, distribution and settlement capabilities. The partnership enables businesses to continue using their existing virtual card programme and booking channels, while participating hotels receive funds through their preferred local payment methods.
The local settlement partner, FCG, connects corporate accommodation demand with hotel supply in China through its distribution technology and hotel relationships. It brings experience supporting corporate travel programmes in China and across Asia Pacific, serving dozens of Chinese state-owned enterprises, including centrally administered enterprises, and more than 100 multinational groups. 
Mainland China’s hotel payment environment operates through established domestic payment methods, including account-to-account transfers and QR-based digital wallets. International businesses using centralised virtual card programmes can encounter hotel payments that fail or require manual workarounds when these payment environments are not connected. Reliance on personal or physical corporate cards can reduce finance teams’ control and visibility, complicate reconciliation and leave travellers temporarily out of pocket.
The new capability extends Conferma Connect to support local settlement at around 32,000 participating hotels in mainland China. It is designed to reduce manual payment friction for travel managers and finance teams and improve spend visibility. Where Conferma’s invoice collection, validation and matching service, Snap+, is enabled, line-item invoice data can also support automated reconciliation.
Travellers can continue booking through established channels. For participating hotels in mainland China, the partnership connects those bookings to local settlement rather than requiring businesses to adopt a separate payment process for covered hotel charges.
FCG contributes hotel payment connectivity and local settlement capabilities, enabling international corporate virtual card payments to reach participating hotels in mainland China through their existing payment processes.
Adam Williams, Head of Commercial (APAC) at Conferma, said: “Inbound international travel to mainland China is an important part of many corporate travel programmes, but the local payment environment is different to many other markets. Through our partnership with FCG, we’re bridging the gap between existing virtual card programmes and the local settlement processes participating hotels in mainland China use today, helping businesses retain their payment controls and visibility.”

title: UK Shoppers Spread Black Friday Spending Across November as Europe Sees Bigger Single-Day Sales Spikes
summary:
UK shoppers have moved past the Black Friday hype, while consumers across mainland Europe continue to concentrate their spending into a single day. According to transaction data released today by European payment services provider Mollie, Black Friday payments in the UK rose 93% on a typical October Friday, compared with sharper spikes in France (+140%), Switzerland (+134%), Austria (+130%) and Germany (+124%). Mollie’s four-year analysis also shows that fears of a post-sale wave of refunds are unfounded.
Comparing Black Friday transactions with an average October Friday, Mollie tracked payment volume across key European markets. While British checkouts saw a +93% increase, shoppers on the continent recorded sharper single-day surges: France led at +140%, followed closely by Switzerland (+134%), Austria (+130%), and Germany (+124%).
"As the pioneer of Black Friday in Europe, the UK market has matured past the initial hype cycle," says Bernardo Caldas, Director of Data at Mollie. “British consumers treat Black Friday as a planned seasonal event, and retailers have diffused the single-day pressure by stretching campaigns across 'Black November'. In contrast, continental markets like France and DACH still experience a dramatic, compressed peak on the day itself.”
Data busts the 'return tsunami' myth
Alongside payment peaks, Mollie analysed four years of merchant refund data to test whether heavy discounting leads to an inevitable wave of product returns. The data shows those fears are unfounded. Mollie’s analysis of 60-day refund rates across more than 120,000 European merchants proves this fear is largely unfounded. On Black Friday 2025, more than 96% of purchases were kept, compared with 97.5% on a typical October Friday. When it comes to fashion, Black Friday purchases were no more likely to be refunded than those made on a typical Friday (and slightly less likely in the past three years).
"There is a persistent narrative that post-sale return hangovers erode peak margins," concludes Caldas. "In reality, purchase commitment remains exceptionally high across both the UK and Europe. Shoppers are taking advantage of discounts with deliberate purchase intent."

title: HyroTrader Adds Hyro Core From $9 and No-Evaluation Hyro Instant to Rebuilt Crypto Prop Platform
summary: The new accounts follow an October overhaul that brought the firm’s own trading terminal, AI-agent trading, BloFin and static loss limits on every challenge   DUBAI, UAE, November 2026: HyroTrader, a crypto proprietary trading firm, has launched two new ways to get a funded trading account. Hyro Core is a one-phase challenge from $9, and Hyro Instant skips the challenge altogether. Both went on sale on 4 November 2026.   They are the second step of a rebuild that began in October. That month HyroTrader launched its own trading terminal with stock and index contracts and opened accounts on it to AI trading agents. It also added BloFin as a second exchange, made every loss limit static and made its payouts easier to verify on a public dashboard.   Firms like HyroTrader give traders a funded account and pay them a share of the profit made on it. Traders usually earn that account by passing a paid trading test, known as a challenge.   At HyroTrader, every account, funded or not, is a simulated (demo) account running on live market data. The payouts are real money, paid as a share of the simulated profit.   Hyro Instant is the bigger change for a firm that until now funded only traders who passed a challenge.   “Without an evaluation, a firm cannot establish whether a trader has a consistent track record or simply had a few successful trades,” HyroTrader said in announcing Hyro Instant. “Nevertheless, the demand for a faster route is clear.”   Hyro Core is the firm’s lowest-priced challenge. A $2,500 account costs $9, and the largest, $100,000, costs $349. Against One-Step, the firm’s other one-phase challenge, it pairs the lower price with tighter loss limits.   To pass, a trader needs a 10% profit over at least four trading days, with no single day counting for more than 40% of it. The challenge ends if the account loses more than 3% of its starting balance in a day, or 5% in total. Both limits are static, which means they stay fixed to the starting balance and do not rise as the account gains.   Funded Hyro Core traders receive a fixed 80% of the profit as payouts. The fee is not refunded once the challenge is activated.   “A trader’s budget does not necessarily reflect their motivation or skill,” HyroTrader said in announcing Hyro Core.   Hyro Instant, a funded account with no evaluation. Image: HyroTrader   Hyro Instant has no test at all. After identity verification and account setup, the trader receives a funded account with no profit target to reach. It costs from $169 for a $5,000 account to $2,799 for $100,000.   It keeps Hyro Core’s daily and total loss limits and adds a per-trade limit. No single trade may lose more than 2% of the starting balance. A first breach of that trade limit brings a warning, and a second closes the account.   The first payout opens after three qualifying trading days (days on which the trader closes at least one trade above set size and price-move thresholds), with the account in profit. The profit split starts at 80% and can rise to 90% at the firm’s discretion. The fee is refunded only if identity verification is not approved.   Both new accounts run on what HyroTrader built in October. At the centre is the Hyro platform, the firm’s own trading terminal, which needs no exchange account. It offers more than 700 perpetual futures markets (contracts with no expiry date) on live prices. Besides crypto, they include contracts on stocks such as Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, on the S&P 500, and on gold and silver.   Traders who prefer an exchange can instead run any programme on their own demo account at Bybit or, since October, at BloFin. HyroTrader says that in 2023 it became the first crypto prop firm to let traders run a challenge on their own exchange demo account.   On the Hyro platform, Hyro Instant accounts included, traders can also connect their own AI agent through MCP, the Model Context Protocol (an open standard for linking AI tools to other software). The agent places trades for the trader’s own strategy under the account’s usual rules, and the trader can revoke its access at any time.   The October rebuild also made payouts easier to check. HyroTrader lists the payouts it sends on the Solana blockchain on a public transparency page, each with a link to its blockchain record unless the trader has chosen to hide it. In November the minimum payout fell from $100 to $25.   The firm also eased its existing challenges in the same week. One-Step challenges bought from 5 November need at least three trading days instead of five and allow an 8% total loss limit instead of 6%. Two-Step challenges bought from 4 November need four trading days in each phase instead of five.   About HyroTrader HyroTrader is a crypto prop firm launched in 2023 and operating from Dubai, UAE. Traders take a challenge or start funded with Hyro Instant, receive 80% of their profits as payouts, up to 90% on some programmes, and are usually paid in stablecoins within 24 hours.   According to HyroTrader’s public payout transparency page, the firm has paid more than $9.5 million in profit splits to traders since 2023, as of November 2026. More than $1.6 million of that went out on the Solana blockchain. HyroTrader says it has funded more than 1,700 traders.   HyroTrader is not a broker and does not provide investment services or advice. All trading takes place on simulated accounts.   Media contact HyroTrader support@hyrotrader.com www.hyrotrader.com

title: Vero Security Raises $11M to Shape How AI Security Engineering Is Done
summary:
Vero Security, which is building the platform for AI Security Engineering, today announced $11 million in seed funding. AI Security Engineering, the work of securing the AI tools and agents employees use, is quickly becoming its own discipline, but at most large enterprises the job is held by someone who already has another role. Vero helps them by doing the ongoing work. Security teams define the policy, and Vero turns it into enforced controls, automatically updates those controls as AI vendors change their tools, and brings the team only the decisions that need a person to make a call. The company is also launching AISecurityEngineering.org, an open community for the people leading this emerging field.
Founded in 2025, Vero already counts multiple Fortune 500 companies among its customers. The round was led by TLV Partners, with participation from GTM Capital, Maple Capital and angel investors.
The organizational shift is already underway. Recent research from IANS and Artico Search found that 65% of companies with at least $10 billion in revenue had assigned someone to lead AI security, but only 18% had made it a dedicated role. At the rest of the organizations surveyed, it was added to an existing leader’s job. Whoever holds it faces a moving target. Employees adopt new AI tools and agents, connect them to enterprise systems and grant them permissions to access sensitive data and take actions. At the same time, AI vendors continuously introduce new capabilities, models, plugins and integrations that can change the security implications of existing configurations.
“CISOs have seen enough dashboards and tables that tell their teams what's wrong and leave the work to them. AI Security Engineering deserves a better operating model, designed for AI rather than borrowed from other areas of security,” said Elad Tessler, Co-Founder and CEO of Vero Security. “We're working alongside the first generation of AI security leaders and building Vero around what they actually need: a platform that does the work, keeps protections current as AI changes, and brings them only the decisions that require human judgment.”
A new discipline needs more than new technology. The professionals taking on AI security are defining the role as they go, with few established playbooks or formal training paths. To help build that foundation, Vero is launching AISecurityEngineering.org, an open community and knowledge center featuring practical field guides, workshops and the ASE credential track.
At the core of Vero's platform is its AI Runtime Governor, designed to put security decisions into effect as AI operates. Its runtime controls inspect supported prompts, tool calls and agent actions, enforcing approved policies at the moment an action is attempted. Vero can stop a coding agent from reading secrets it has no reason to touch, block agent actions that violate security policies and keep malicious skills or prompt injection from triggering unauthorized behavior.
These protections are applied during execution, without waiting for manual security review.
Vero works through the endpoint, identity, AI and security tools a company already runs, so employees have nothing new to install. It combines continuous discovery with its own security analysis and runtime enforcement, maintaining visibility into AI tools, agents, connected systems, configurations and permissions, and giving security professionals the context to understand risks and define effective protections.
The platform also carries security decisions through to execution. Security teams establish policies and determine which changes Vero can handle automatically. Vero implements approved controls, coordinates remediation with relevant owners, verifies completion and keeps protections aligned as the environment evolves. When a change requires a new risk decision, Vero brings the analysis and recommended action to the responsible security professional.
One decision from the security team can mean dozens of controls behind the scenes. A new Fortune 1000 customer, for example, began its Vero deployment with a simple policy: only developers could connect AI agents to corporate code repositories or allow them to execute code. Within minutes, Vero translated that single decision into more than 15 security controls across coding agents, MCP servers, skills, identities and runtime actions, automatically putting them into effect across the organization. As AI tools and capabilities evolve, Vero continuously adjusts those controls to keep the original policy enforced.
“AI Security Engineering is becoming a core responsibility inside enterprise security organizations,” said Rona Segev, Co-Founder & Managing Partner at TLV Partners, which led the round. “The professionals taking on that responsibility need technology designed for the pace and complexity of AI. Vero is bringing security expertise, continuous execution and runtime enforcement together in a platform built for how this new discipline needs to operate.”
GTM Capital invested following a structured evaluation with its community of Fortune 500 CIOs and CISOs, who worked directly with Vero before the firm committed.
“AI is becoming a new attack surface in the enterprise, and we're hearing directly from CISOs how quickly AI Security Engineering is becoming a distinct responsibility,” said Saqib Awan, Founder and Managing Director at GTM Capital. “We evaluated dozens of companies in this space. Vero stood out because it's building technology that helps security professionals do the work, from understanding risks to enforcing protections. It's GTM Capital's first investment in an Israeli-founded cybersecurity company since Cyera.”
Vero was founded by Elad Tessler (CEO) and Daniel Meirov (CTO). Tessler previously led product at Astrix Security, acquired by Cisco in 2026. Meirov was the first employee at Sightfull, where he led R&D and product. The two met in Unit 8200, where they co-led a cyber operations unit of more than 100 people.
The company will use the funding to advance its AI Security Engineering platform, expand coverage across enterprise AI technologies and security workflows, and grow its go-to-market presence in the United States.

title: Growing Payments Complexity Putting Friction Back Into Ecommerce, Ravelin Report Finds
summary:
Ecommerce merchants risk frustrating customers and losing sales by imposing stricter than necessary payment security checks, according to new research from fraud prevention specialist Ravelin.  
The growth of alternative payment methods and agentic commerce may encourage merchants to tighten fraud controls further. Ravelin argues they should instead get better at understanding which transactions need authentication checks, and which are safe to be left alone.
Ravelin's Payments Authentication & Risk Report 2027 is based on millions of transactions across 37 countries. It finds that over four-fifths of transactions (82%) globally successfully passed 3D Secure (3DS) authentication. However, more customers are experiencing interruptions at checkout, as they are asked to complete additional security checks.
According to Ravelin, the share of frictionless transactions (those completed without interruption) has fallen by five percent to 53% over the past year. The proportion of successfully completed 3D Secure (3DS) payment challenges has risen by eight percent to 84%. 
3DS helps lower fraud from payment cards and allows merchants to avoid financial liability for accepting payments that customers later report as fraudulent. However, 3DS challenges, such as asking for extra passwords or authorization via banking apps, increase the chances shoppers abandon their shopping baskets before paying, potentially impacting revenues. 
Ravelin finds that merchants and payment service providers (PSPs) may be applying 3DS challenges more broadly than they need, in response to growing fraud threats and growing scrutiny from banks and card issuers. 
Ravelin’s payments experts argue that merchants and payment service providers should make better use of their data and 3DS flows to distinguish between higher and lower-risk transactions. Doing so would enable them to accept more payments with confidence and remove unnecessary steps from customer journeys.
UK leads the way, France struggles
Ravelin's Payments Authentication & Risk Report 2027 highlights significant differences in how successfully merchants in different markets balance security with a smooth customer experience.
The UK performs particularly well, ranking first globally for overall 3D Secure (3DS) authentication success at 94%, first, tied with Poland, for successful security challenges at 93%, and second for frictionless transactions at 72%.
France, by contrast, has an overall authentication success rate of 90%, but just 31% of transactions are frictionless, the second-lowest proportion among the countries reported on.
Since January 2026, France has required virtually all transactions to pass through 3DS by law. 
The wider European picture reflects a similar trend. Successful completion of additional security challenges has increased from 75% to 85%, but the proportion of frictionless transactions has declined.
Martin Sweeney, CEO at Ravelin, said: “Payment security is essential. But several factors are putting more friction into online shopping – from the growth of agentic commerce and the evolving fraud landscape, to more cautious banks and tighter authentication requirements.
“Blindly putting more transactions through security checks isn't the best response. The key is assessing when additional verification is needed and when legitimate customers can complete their purchases without interruption.
“Getting that balance right means protecting businesses against fraud and keeping them compliant with authorization mandates – without putting unnecessary obstacles in customers’ way."
Alternative payment methods continue to gain ground 
The report also highlights the continuing rise in popularity of alternative payment methods.  
Digital wallets, including Apple Pay and Google Pay, are now the most popular payment method in 16 of the 37 countries analyzed, while traditional credit and debit cards remain the leading choice for 18 countries. 
Account-to-account (A2A) payments, which allow customers to make payments directly from their bank accounts, have also gained ground. They now rank among the three most popular payment methods in four countries: Belgium, Brazil, the Netherlands and Poland. The share of payments is set to rise in Europe as Wero, the European Payments Initiative’s A2A service, gains momentum across the continent.
Sweeney added: "New ways of paying, like A2A payments, are gaining ground across Europe – with Wero expected to change payment habits across the continent.
“For merchants and PSPs, the priority isn't simply offering customers more ways to pay. It's making sure those payments are secure, straightforward and as seamless as possible."

title: Ecommpay Offers Free Payment Performance Assessments to Help Businesses Tackle Avoidable Declines This Festive Season
summary:
Personalised review and online consultation with Business Growth Specialist open to businesses using any payment provider
To help merchants ensure their payments options are optimised for the festive trading season, inclusive global payments platform, Ecommpay, has launched free payment performance assessments. The offer combines a preliminary review of submitted payment data with a 30-minute specialist consultation, giving merchants a personalised perspective on where their checkout could perform better.
Following examination of payment data, Ecommpay will explore patterns behind declined payments and highlight potential opportunities to improve acceptance rates without compromising security. A 30-minute online session with Daniella Sjarki, Ecommpay’s Business Growth Specialist, will help the merchant understand their payment declines, agree opportunities worth exploring and identify practical next steps.
Daniella Sjarki explained: “Every genuine sale is important during peak trading such as Black Friday, Christmas and New Year – but avoidable payment declines can mean missed sales.  To protect profitability, businesses need a clearer view of what their payment data is telling them. A decline rate alone does not explain what is happening or what to do next. This assessment is about taking a closer look together, identifying questions worth investigating and helping merchants prioritise practical next steps.”
Open to existing Ecommpay merchants and businesses using other payment providers, the assessment is designed to provide vital clarity and direction. There is no charge for the preliminary review or consultation, and no obligation to switch providers. Ecommpay’s standard fees apply to any payment services subsequently agreed.
Businesses will be asked to share relevant payment information, including their acceptance rate and main decline reasons, where available. These will then be reviewed ahead of a tailored online discussion. Participants will receive a short summary afterwards to share with their teams in order to guide further action.

title: Sumsub Launches Google Address Verification to Confirm Businesses Operate Where They Claim
summary:
Sumsub, the first AI-powered trust infrastructure for compliance operations at scale, today launched Google Address Verification, a new capability that checks whether a business actually operates at the address it declares. 
Using Google Maps and Places data, the solution confirms whether a location exists, whether the business trades there under its declared name, and whether public signals and a consistent business presence support its legitimacy. It is built for business risk assessment and operational validation, and helps payment providers, marketplaces, logistics operators and B2B lenders spot fake merchants and shell businesses before onboarding them.
Verifying operational reality, not just registration
Standard Know Your Business (KYB) checks confirm that a company is legally registered and that its documents are valid. Legal registration doesn’t prove that a business is operating, though, or that it trades from the address it has declared. For platforms that depend on physical merchants, such as restaurants listed on delivery apps, retailers accepting card payments, or suppliers dispatching goods, that gap leaves room for fake merchants, shell businesses and fraudulent onboarding attempts.
Google Address Verification closes that gap by comparing a business’s declared details with real-world location data. Checks run without asking the applicant for documents first. Legitimate businesses face less friction, and inconsistencies are flagged for review. Results feed into Sumsub’s wider platform, which connects business verification, fraud prevention, transaction monitoring and risk workflows.
“A company can be properly registered and still not be trading from the address on its paperwork,” said Andrew Novoselsky, Chief Product Officer at Sumsub. “For businesses that onboard merchants, deliver to them or lend to them, that is the question that matters. Google Address Verification lets them check a business’s real-world presence at the start of onboarding, without asking for documents first, and fall back to traditional proof of address only when the data isn’t conclusive. Genuine businesses get approved faster, and fake ones are easier to spot before they’re on the platform.”
Core capabilities
Location and trade name validation: Confirms that the declared address exists, that a business is listed there under the declared trade name, and that its declared identity matches its publicly visible one.
Public business signals for risk scoring: Uses location consistency as additional merchant risk indicators.
Operational feasibility checks: Assesses whether a location can realistically support the activity a business declares, such as receiving deliveries or dispatching goods.
Layered verification: The depth of public business listings varies by market and by type of business. Where listing data is limited or inconclusive, applicants can confirm their address with a utility bill, lease agreement, corporate address document or other proof of occupancy. Every business has a clear route to verification.
Use cases across industries
Google Address Verification is designed for three main groups:
Retail and merchant networks: Payment providers, merchant acquirers, POS providers, B2B marketplaces, consumer goods distributors and franchise networks can confirm that a merchant operates from its declared location before approving it.
Logistics and delivery: Courier services, freight platforms, warehouse aggregators and last-mile delivery providers can confirm that a business location is credible for pickups and drop-offs.
B2B lending: Merchant financing, invoice financing, trade finance and B2B BNPL providers can get additional evidence that a business is operational before extending credit.
